flashcards.q: Describe the classloader delegation model and why it exists.
flashcards.a: Bootstrap -> platform -> application, each delegating to its parent first before loading itself. Exists to guarantee core JDK classes always resolve to the trusted bootstrap-loaded version regardless of what an application defines with the same name -- a security/correctness boundary.

flashcards.q: Walk through tiered compilation: interpreter, C1, C2. Why not always use C2?
flashcards.a: Interpreter: zero compile latency, slow dispatch. C1: fast compile, light opt, gathers profiling data once a method warms. C2: slow compile, aggressive opt (inlining, escape analysis) once truly hot. Always using C2 would give best eventual throughput but terrible warmup latency since C2 compilation is comparatively slow.

flashcards.q: What happens when a C2-compiled method's speculative assumption breaks?
flashcards.a: Deoptimization: the JVM discards the compiled code, falls back to interpreting, and may eventually re-profile and recompile with corrected assumptions. Can thrash ('deopt storm') if the pattern is genuinely unstable, e.g. a call site alternating types.

flashcards.q: What is escape analysis and what two optimizations does it enable?
flashcards.a: C2-tier analysis proving an object never escapes its allocating method/thread. Non-escape past the method -> scalar replacement (fields become locals/registers, zero heap allocation, zero GC cost). Non-escape past the thread -> lock elision (synchronized removed since no contention is possible).

flashcards.q: Why is escape analysis only available at the C2 tier, not the interpreter or C1?
flashcards.a: It requires expensive whole-method (often cross-call, with inlining) data-flow analysis to prove non-escape -- exactly the kind of slow, deep analysis reserved for C2's optimization budget once a method has proven itself hot; C1 prioritizes fast compile time instead.

flashcards.q: Compare G1 and generational ZGC on pause time, throughput, and memory.
flashcards.a: G1: region-based, collects highest-garbage regions first, configurable pause goal (commonly tens of ms), still has real stop-the-world phases. ZGC (generational, Java 25 LTS default/only form): sub-ms pauses (~0.1-0.5ms) independent of heap size, but no compressed oops (~15-30% more memory) and ~5-15% lower throughput than G1.

flashcards.q: How does ZGC achieve sub-millisecond pauses regardless of heap size?
flashcards.a: Does marking, relocation, and remapping almost entirely concurrently with running application threads, using colored pointers (GC metadata embedded in unused reference bits) and load barriers (transparently redirect access to mid-relocation objects).

flashcards.q: What is a humongous object in G1 and why is it a real gotcha?
flashcards.a: An object larger than 50% of a region size, allocated specially across contiguous regions instead of a normal region. Frequent large allocations (big arrays, big collections) cause additional GC pressure and fragmentation from this special-cased handling.

flashcards.q: What's the 2026 default guidance for choosing G1 vs generational ZGC?
flashcards.a: G1 for most general-purpose services (predictable, well-understood, resource-efficient). Generational ZGC specifically for large-heap, latency-SLO-bound services where sub-millisecond pause consistency matters more than the memory/throughput cost.

flashcards.q: Why does a JVM microbenchmark appear to 'get faster' over its first several thousand calls?
flashcards.a: JIT warmup -- early calls run interpreted or C1-compiled (slower), and once the method crosses C2's invocation threshold and gets recompiled with aggressive optimization, it stabilizes at steady-state C2-optimized performance. Use JMH, not a naive hand-rolled timing loop, to measure this correctly.

flashcards.q: How does JMH avoid the measurement pitfalls of a hand-rolled timing loop?
flashcards.a: It explicitly separates warmup iterations (discarded, let the JIT reach steady state) from measurement iterations, and guards against dead-code elimination and constant-folding of benchmark inputs via blackholes -- none of which a raw System.nanoTime() loop protects against.

flashcards.q: What causes a classloader leak in a service that dynamically loads/reloads classes?
flashcards.a: Something (a static field, a ThreadLocal, a lingering thread) still references an instance or class from an old classloader after redeploy, keeping the entire loaded-class graph alive indefinitely and eventually causing OutOfMemoryError: Metaspace.

flashcards.q: What is carrier-thread pinning with virtual threads (Project Loom), and what's the fix?
flashcards.a: A virtual thread inside a synchronized block can't unmount from its carrier thread when it blocks, since monitor ownership can't safely migrate carriers mid-hold — under load this starves the limited carrier pool. Fix: replace synchronized with ReentrantLock around the blocking call; locate pinning with -Djdk.tracePinnedThreads=full or JFR pinning events.

flashcards.q: How do you confirm a Metaspace growth pattern is a classloader leak rather than legitimate dynamic class generation churn?
flashcards.a: Take heap dumps across two redeploys and diff classloader instance counts (Eclipse MAT has a dedicated classloader-leak report) — a count that grows by roughly one per redeploy and never drops is the leak signature; a framework properly releasing old classes on redeploy shows churn, not accumulation.

flashcards.q: Why isn't volatile a substitute for synchronized/AtomicInteger for a multi-threaded counter?
flashcards.a: volatile guarantees happens-before visibility/ordering for each individual read and write of that field, but no mutual exclusion — a compound read-modify-write (increment) can still race between threads exactly like CPython's x += 1, since volatile never made the multi-step operation atomic.
